speaker: Mitchell Hashimoto
title: Mitchell Hashimoto’s new way of writing code
question: In enterprise software, why do unified platforms that bundle multiple infrastructure tools often fail to sell even to companies already using those tools?
guest: We had this first commercial product called Atlas, and the idea was commercially shipping the vision of running all the products. There were a couple death knells there. One of them was that you had to run all the products, so if you were just a Vault user, you had a really impossible time buying into our commercial product. And the second was that regardless of the adoption required, you're trying to solve a problem that multiple different buying organizations in a company were fighting over. Even with people who had adopted all our tools, we ran into the problem of who pays for it. One of the tough lessons I had to learn is that companies want to pay for software, but they will fight over whose budget owns that. The budget has to exist, and if it looks like a networking problem, they're going to say, 'Oh, networking should pay for that, so I have more budget to buy my other toys that I want.' We had this product where it was like: does security pay for it, does networking pay for it, does infrastructure pay for it, does dev tooling pay for it? It's just that Spider-Man meme where everyone's pointing at each other, and ultimately you don't sell anything.

points.core: Requiring full-suite adoption blocks customers who only use one underlying tool.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Unified platforms usually fail because the way enterprises buy and run infrastructure doesn't match the way the bundle is packaged, even when the technical fit is real.

Each tool in the bundle typically has a different owner, budget, and renewal cycle: the database team, the security team, and the platform team each chose their tool separately. A unified platform has no single buyer with the authority or budget to purchase it, so the sale requires cross-team consensus that nobody is motivated to lead.

The value proposition is also weak for existing users. They have already paid the integration cost, building glue code, runbooks, and expertise around their current setup. The bundle solves a problem they've already solved, while asking them to accept migration risk for infrastructure that currently works.

Bundles also tend to be weaker than best-of-breed tools in each category, so every specialist team sees a downgrade in their own area. Add fears of vendor lock-in and concentrated blast radius, and the "savings" from consolidation rarely outweigh the perceived risk.

Bundles tend to succeed mainly with new buyers who haven't integrated anything yet, or when a senior executive mandates consolidation for cost reasons.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Even when an enterprise already runs the underlying tools, buying a unified platform collides with how large organizations budget, govern, and operate infrastructure. Individual tools usually sit under separate teams and cost centers—security owning secrets, platform engineering owning provisioning, SRE owning observability—so no single buyer holds both the mandate and the combined budget to sign an umbrella contract. Pitching the bundle turns a departmental purchase into a slow, political cross-functional negotiation where any team can veto the deal, especially when incumbent subscriptions renew on staggered multi-year cycles. Moreover, teams running those tools in production have already absorbed the integration cost by building custom glue code, workflows, and access controls around them; adopting a vendor’s opinionated control plane introduces migration risk and rework rather than saving effort. Finally, usage across the bundle is rarely uniform, leaving procurement reluctant to pay platform premiums for partial shelfware and deeper vendor lock-in when licensing or upgrading just one bottlenecked tool solves the immediate pain.

noweb.answer:
Unified infrastructure platforms often fail to sell to existing users because enterprise org charts and budgets mirror individual tools rather than integrated workflows. Networking, security, data, and DevOps teams hold separate budgets and buying authority, meaning no single leader has both the mandate and the funding to purchase a cross-cutting bundle. Closing a deal therefore requires consensus across multiple department heads—often across staggered contract renewal dates—turning routine renewals into slow, political procurement cycles.

Furthermore, companies running those standalone tools have already paid the integration tax. Their engineers have built custom scripts, pipelines, and access controls to glue the components together, so migrating working systems onto an opinionated platform introduces operational risk and switching toil without delivering net-new capabilities. Practitioners also resist losing granular configurability, as unified layers frequently abstract away power-user features while deepening single-vendor lock-in. Ultimately, these platforms pitch integration convenience to organizations that have already solved integration internally and lack a single buyer empowered to pay for it.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Unified platforms usually fail because the problem they solve isn't owned by anyone who holds a budget. In most enterprises each tool was bought by a different team, such as security, data engineering, DevOps, or networking. Each team has its own budget, its own vendor relationships, and its own preferred product. The pain of stitching those tools together is spread across the organization, so no single buyer feels it strongly enough to sponsor a consolidated purchase.

The pitch also asks buyers to replace systems that already work. Those tools are wired into workflows, scripts, compliance processes, and people's skills, so the cost and risk of migrating are immediate and concrete. The benefits of integration are speculative and arrive later. Each team also compares the bundle's version of its tool against the best standalone product it already uses, and the bundle's component is often weaker. Buyers also worry about lock-in and about one vendor becoming a single point of failure.

Platforms tend to succeed when they first win one painful use case outright and then expand into neighboring tools, rather than selling the whole bundle up front.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Unified infrastructure platforms often stall in enterprise sales because enterprise buying rarely mirrors technical architecture. Even when a company already uses every category of tool in the bundle, those tools are typically owned by separate teams with distinct budgets, procurement timelines, and success metrics. Selling a unified platform forces a vendor to orchestrate cross-departmental consensus among buyers who have little incentive to surrender autonomy or pool their budgets.

Compounding this organizational friction is the asymmetry of switching risk. Replacing several working point solutions simultaneously means unwinding custom integrations, retraining multiple teams, and navigating staggered multi-year contracts, all while taking on concentrated vendor lock-in. Each individual team also tends to perceive a bundled suite as a downgrade from its specialized, best-of-breed tool, making them reluctant to absorb migration pain for a company-wide benefit they do not directly feel. As a result, buyers usually prefer to renew familiar standalone tools incrementally rather than champion a politically expensive, all-or-nothing consolidation.

A company can use every tool in a bundle without having a single buyer for the platform. Networking, security, and operations teams may each own their tools, budgets, and renewal schedules. A platform deal asks those teams to agree on funding, ownership, and rollout, even when each team is satisfied with what it already uses.

Existing adoption also raises the bar for the sale. The vendor has to show what unifying the tools adds beyond what the customer already gets from them. Savings from one contract or a shared console may be too small to justify migrating workflows, retraining staff, or depending more heavily on one vendor. The deal often stalls because the benefits are spread across the company while the cost and risk land on the individual teams that have to approve it.

A company can use every tool in a bundle and still have no single buyer for the platform. Different teams often chose the tools, own their budgets, and renew contracts at different times. Each team can justify paying for a tool that works. Buying the platform requires someone to coordinate those teams and show that switching is worth the cost and risk.

The bundle sells when integration solves a shared problem that someone owns. For example, if engineers lose hours tracing outages across separate tools, a platform that measurably shortens recovery gives an infrastructure leader a reason to buy. Without that payoff, renewing each tool is usually the easier decision.
